cor-block-diagonalization.title: Block Diagonalization by a Sylvester Solution
cor-block-diagonalization.title_html: Block Diagonalization by a Sylvester Solution
cor-block-diagonalization.html:
Let A∈Mm(F), B∈Mn(F) and C∈Mm×n(F), and put M=(AC0B)∈Mm+n(F).

  1. If X∈Mm×n(F) satisfies AX−XB=−C, then with P=(ImX0In) we have P−1MP=A⊕B. In particular M∼A⊕B.
  2. Conversely, if P−1MP=A⊕B for some X∈Mm×n(F) and the matrix P built from it as in (a), then that X satisfies AX−XB=−C.
  3. If F=C and spec(A)∩spec(B)=∅, then a solution X exists, and it is unique; so M∼A⊕B for every corner C.

cor-circulants-algebra.title: Circulants Form a Commutative Algebra
cor-circulants-algebra.html:
Let Cn⊆Mn(C) be the set of circulants of size n. Then:

  1. Cn is a subspace of Mn(C) of dimension n, with basis I,S,…,Sn−1;
  2. Cn is closed under products, and any two of its members commute;
  3. A∈Cn if and only if F∗AF is diagonal;
  4. a circulant C is invertible if and only if pc(ωj)≠0 for every j, and then C−1 is again a circulant.

cor-commutant-block-diagonal.title: Disjoint Spectra Split the Commutant
cor-commutant-block-diagonal.html: Let A1∈Mn1(C),…,Ar∈Mnr(C) have pairwise disjoint spectra, and put D=A1⊕⋯⊕Ar∈MN(C), N=n1+⋯+nr. Let Z∈MN(C) satisfy DZ=ZD, and partition Z into blocks Zpq∈Mnp×nq(C) for the partition N=n1+⋯+nr. Then Zpq=0for all p≠q, so Z=Z11⊕⋯⊕Zrr is block diagonal, and each diagonal block satisfies ApZpp=ZppAp.

cor-det-product-eigenvalues-again.title: Determinant Is the Product of the Eigenvalues
cor-det-product-eigenvalues-again.title_html: Determinant Is the Product of the Eigenvalues
cor-det-product-eigenvalues-again.html: Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then detA=λ1⋯λn.

cor-normal-commuting-poly.title: The Adjoint of a Normal Operator Is a Polynomial in It
cor-normal-commuting-poly.title_html: The Adjoint of a Normal Operator Is a Polynomial in It
cor-normal-commuting-poly.html: Let T∈L(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk. Then there is a polynomial p∈C[x] of degree less than k with T∗=p(T).

cor-normal-kernel.title: Kernel, Image and an Orthogonal Splitting
cor-normal-kernel.title_html: Kernel, Image and an Orthogonal Splitting
cor-normal-kernel.html:
Let T∈L(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space V. Then:

  1. kerT=kerT∗;
  2. imT=imT∗;
  3. V=kerT⊕imT, and the two summands are orthogonal to each other.

cor-normal-orthogonal-eigenspaces.title: Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues Are Orthogonal
cor-normal-orthogonal-eigenspaces.title_html: Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues Are Orthogonal
cor-normal-orthogonal-eigenspaces.html: Let T∈L(V) be normal, let λ≠μ be eigenvalues of T, and let Tu=λu and Tv=μv. Then ⟨u,v⟩=0. Hence Eλ(T)⊥Eμ(T) whenever λ≠μ.

cor-normal-spectral-corollaries.title: The Spectrum Decides
cor-normal-spectral-corollaries.html:
Let T∈L(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space.

  1. T is self-adjoint if and only if every eigenvalue of T is real.
  2. T is unitary if and only if every eigenvalue of T has modulus 1.
  3. ⟨Tv,v⟩ is a non-negative real number for every v∈V if and only if every eigenvalue of T is a non-negative real.

cor-schur-matrix.title: Schur Factorization
cor-schur-matrix.html: Let A∈Mn(C) with n≥1, and let λ1,…,λn be the eigenvalues of A, each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any prescribed order. Then there are a unitary U∈Mn(C) and an upper triangular T∈Mn(C) with A=UTU∗,tii=λi(1≤i≤n).

cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby.title: Diagonalizable Matrices Are Everywhere
cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby.html: Let A∈Mn(C) and let ε>0. Then there is a diagonalizable A′∈Mn(C) with |aij−aij′|<εfor all i,j. In this sense every complex square matrix is a limit of diagonalizable ones.

cor-simultaneous-orthogonal-real.title: Commuting Symmetric Matrices
cor-simultaneous-orthogonal-real.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let F⊆L(V) be a non-empty commuting family of self-adjoint operators. Then V has an orthonormal basis of common eigenvectors. Equivalently, if A1,…,Ar∈Mn(R) are symmetric and pairwise commuting, there is Q∈O(n) with every Q⊤AiQ diagonal.

cor-simultaneous-unitary-matrix.title: Commuting Normal Matrices
cor-simultaneous-unitary-matrix.html: Let A1,…,Ar∈Mn(C) be normal and pairwise commuting. Then there is a unitary U∈U(n) such that U∗AiU is diagonal for every i. The same holds for an arbitrary commuting family of normal matrices in Mn(C).

cor-so3-is-rotation.title: Orthogonal Matrices in Dimension Three
cor-so3-is-rotation.html: Let Q∈O(3). Then there are an orthonormal basis (u,w1,w2) of R3 and an angle θ∈[0,π] such that, in that basis, the matrix of TQ is [1]⊕Rθif detQ=1,[−1]⊕Rθif detQ=−1. In particular every Q∈SO(3) fixes the line span(u) pointwise and rotates the plane span(u)⊥ by θ.

cor-spectral-complex-matrix.title: Unitary Diagonalization
cor-spectral-complex-matrix.html: Let A∈Mn(C). Then A is normal if and only if there exist a unitary U∈U(n) and a diagonal D∈Mn(C) with A=UDU∗. A matrix admitting such a factorization is called unitarily diagonalizable. The diagonal of D is the list of eigenvalues of A with multiplicity, in an order that may be prescribed in advance, and the columns of U are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

cor-spectral-real-matrix.title: Orthogonal Diagonalization
cor-spectral-real-matrix.html: Let A∈Mn(R). Then A is symmetric if and only if there are an orthogonal Q∈O(n) and a real diagonal D with A=QDQ⊤. The diagonal of D is the eigenvalue list of A with multiplicity, in any prescribed order, and the columns of Q are a corresponding orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum.title: Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix
cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum.title_html: Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix
cor-symmetric-rank-one-sum.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric, and let (q1,…,qn) be an orthonormal basis of Rn with Aqi=λiqi. Then A=∑i=1nλiqiqi⊤, and each qiqi⊤ is the matrix of the orthogonal projection of Rn onto the line span(qi).

cor-trace-sum-eigenvalues-again.title: Trace Is the Sum of the Eigenvalues
cor-trace-sum-eigenvalues-again.title_html: Trace Is the Sum of the Eigenvalues
cor-trace-sum-eigenvalues-again.html: Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then trA=λ1+⋯+λn.

def-circulant.title: Circulant matrix
def-circulant.html: Let n≥1 and let c=(c0,c1,…,cn−1)∈Cn. The circulant with first row c is the matrix C∈Mn(C) whose entries are (C)jk=ck−j(0≤j,k≤n−1), where the subscript k−j is read modulo n. The polynomial pc(x)=c0+c1x+c2x2+⋯+cn−1xn−1∈C[x] is called the symbol of C.

def-cross-product-matrix.title: Cross-product Matrix
def-cross-product-matrix.html: For n=(n1,n2,n3)∈R3, the cross-product matrix of n is Kn:=(0−n3n2n30−n1−n2n10)∈M3(R), so that Knv=n×v for every v∈R3.

def-departure-from-normality.title: Departure from Normality
def-departure-from-normality.html: Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with algebraic multiplicity. The departure from normality of A is the non-negative real number Δ(A) defined by Δ(A)2:=‖A‖F2−∑i=1n|λi|2.

def-function-of-normal-operator.title: Function of an Operator
def-function-of-normal-operator.html: Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk and spectral resolution T=∑iλiPi. For any function f:spec(T)→F, define f(T):=∑i=1kf(λi)Pi ∈L(V).

def-lyapunov-equation.title: Lyapunov equation
def-lyapunov-equation.html: Let A∈Mn(C) and Q∈Mn(C). The Lyapunov equation for the pair (A,Q) is AX+XA∗=−Q, with unknown X∈Mn(C). Call A stable when every λ∈spec(A) has Reλ<0.

def-spectral-resolution.title: Spectral Resolution
def-spectral-resolution.html: Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), let λ1,…,λk be the distinct eigenvalues of T, and write Ei=Eλi(T) for the corresponding eigenspaces. Let Pi:=PEi∈L(V) be the orthogonal projection onto Ei (@def-orthogonal-projection). The identity T=λ1P1+λ2P2+⋯+λkPk is the spectral resolution of T, and the family (P1,…,Pk) is the resolution of the identity attached to T.

def-sylvester-operator.title: Sylvester operator
def-sylvester-operator.html: Let A∈Mm(F) and B∈Mn(F). The Sylvester operator of the pair (A,B) is SA,B:Mm×n(F)→Mm×n(F),SA,B(X)=AX−XB. The equation AX−XB=C, for a given C∈Mm×n(F), is the Sylvester equation.

eq-normal-row-column.html: ∑i≤j|tij|2=∑k≥j|tjk|2(j=1,…,n).

eq-schur-split.html: ‖A‖F2=‖T‖F2=∑i=1n|tii|2+∑i<j|tij|2=∑i=1n|λi|2+∑i<j|tij|2.

eq-sylvester-kronecker.html: vec(SA,B(X))=KvecX,K:=In⊗A−B⊤⊗Im.

exr-commuting-normal-families-c1.title: C1: A special case of a theorem of Fuglede
exr-commuting-normal-families-c1.title_html: C1: A special case of a theorem of Fuglede
exr-commuting-normal-families-c1.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let S,T∈L(V) be both normal, with ST=TS.

  1. Prove that ST∗=T∗S and S∗T=TS∗.
  2. Deduce that S+T∗ and ST∗ are normal.
  3. Give an example of two commuting operators, not both normal, for which the conclusion of (a) fails as stated for the pair — that is, exhibit commuting S,T with ST∗≠T∗S.

Note on the hypotheses: a theorem of Fuglede says that in (a) the operator S need not be assumed normal — it is enough that T be normal and that S commute with T. That stronger statement is true and is not proved in this book; (a) is only the case in which both are normal, and its proof uses the normality of S in an essential way.

exr-commuting-normal-families-c2.title: C2: A commuting family of orthogonal projections
exr-commuting-normal-families-c2.title_html: C2: A commuting family of orthogonal projections
exr-commuting-normal-families-c2.html:
Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F=R or C, and let P1,…,Pr∈L(V) be the orthogonal projections onto subspaces U1,…,Ur, pairwise commuting.

  1. Prove that there is an orthonormal basis B of V such that every vector of B lies in Ui or in Ui⊥, for every i.
  2. Deduce that PiPj is the orthogonal projection onto Ui∩Uj.
  3. Prove that Pi+Pj is an orthogonal projection if and only if Ui⊥Uj, and identify the subspace in that case.

Hint for (a): the eigenvalues of an idempotent operator.

exr-defect-from-normality-a1.title: A1
exr-defect-from-normality-a1.html:
1. Define the Frobenius norm of a matrix, and give the expression for ‖A‖F2 as a trace.
  2. State @thm-schur-inequality, including the equality case and how the eigenvalues are counted.
  3. Define Δ(A), and say why the definition needs @thm-schur-inequality before it can be made.
  4. True or false: Δ(A) equals the Frobenius distance from A to the nearest normal matrix. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if A and B are similar then Δ(A)=Δ(B). Justify your answer.
  6. Name the two facts about the Frobenius norm and about triangular matrices that the proof of @thm-schur-inequality rests on.

exr-defect-from-normality-b1.title: B1: Computing the defect
exr-defect-from-normality-b1.html:
For each matrix below, compute ‖A‖F2, the eigenvalue list, and Δ(A). State in each case whether the matrix is normal, and say how you know without multiplying A by A∗.

  1. (3405)
  2. (11−11)
  3. J3(2)
  4. (010001100)

exr-defect-from-normality-b2.title: B2: Verifying Schur’s inequality
exr-defect-from-normality-b2.html:
Let A=(111021003).

  1. Compute both sides of @thm-schur-inequality for A and verify the inequality.
  2. Hence determine whether A is normal, without computing A∗A or AA∗.
  3. Write down a normal matrix N with ‖A−N‖F=Δ(A), and verify the equality.

exr-defect-from-normality-b3.title: B3: The nearest symmetric matrix
exr-defect-from-normality-b3.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) and write S=12(A+A⊤) and W=12(A−A⊤), so that A=S+W with S⊤=S and W⊤=−W.

  1. Prove that ⟨B,C⟩=0 in the Frobenius inner product whenever B∈Mn(R) is symmetric and C∈Mn(R) is skew-symmetric.
  2. Deduce that ‖A−B‖F≥‖W‖F for every symmetric B∈Mn(R), with equality only for B=S. Hence S is the nearest symmetric matrix to A.
  3. Carry this out for A=(240−2), and compare the resulting distance with Δ(A).

exr-defect-from-normality-c1.title: C1: Unitary similarity preserves the defect, ordinary similarity does not
exr-defect-from-normality-c1.title_html:
C1: Unitary similarity preserves the defect, ordinary similarity does
not
exr-defect-from-normality-c1.html:
1. Prove that Δ(U∗AU)=Δ(A) for every A∈Mn(C) and every unitary U.
  2. Give A,B∈M2(C) that are similar with Δ(A)≠Δ(B), exhibiting an explicit P with P−1AP=B.
  3. Deduce that two similar matrices with different defects cannot be unitarily similar, and use this to show that (1102) and diag(1,2) are not unitarily similar.

exr-defect-from-normality-c2.title: C2: Equality plus a single eigenvalue forces a scalar
exr-defect-from-normality-c2.title_html: C2: Equality plus a single eigenvalue forces a scalar
exr-defect-from-normality-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) satisfy ‖A‖F2=∑i=1n|λi|2, and suppose A has only one distinct eigenvalue λ, so that pA=(x−λ)n.

  1. Prove that A=λI.
  2. Deduce that a normal matrix whose characteristic polynomial is xn is the zero matrix.
  3. Show that the hypothesis of equality cannot be dropped, by computing Δ for a matrix with pA=(x−λ)n that is not λI.

exr-defect-from-normality-c3.title: C3: The commutator is at least as big as the defect squared
exr-defect-from-normality-c3.title_html: C3: The commutator is at least as big as the defect squared
exr-defect-from-normality-c3.html:
For A∈Mn(C) write [A,A∗]=AA∗−A∗A.

  1. Prove that ‖[A,A∗]‖F is unchanged when A is replaced by U∗AU with U unitary.
  2. Let T=(λ1b0λ2). Compute [T,T∗] and show that ‖[T,T∗]‖F2=2|b|4+2|b|2|λ1−λ2|2.
  3. Deduce that every A∈M2(C) satisfies ‖[A,A∗]‖F≥2Δ(A)2, and determine exactly when equality holds.

Hint for (c): Schur-triangularize, and use (a) to move the computation to the triangular factor.

exr-normal-operators-a1.title: A1
exr-normal-operators-a1.html:
1. State the definition of a normal operator, and state one equivalent condition phrased in terms of norms.
  2. True or false: every self-adjoint operator is normal, and every normal operator is self-adjoint. Justify both halves.
  3. Let T be normal with Tv=3v. What is T∗v? What if Tv=3iv?
  4. Give a normal operator on R2 that is neither self-adjoint nor unitary.
  5. True or false: if S and T are normal then S+T is normal. Justify your answer.
  6. Explain in one sentence why a normal operator cannot be nilpotent unless it is zero.

exr-normal-operators-b1.title: B1: Determine which are normal
exr-normal-operators-b1.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are normal, with the standard inner product. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a vector v with ‖Av‖≠‖A∗v‖.

  1. (1111) over R.
  2. (1101) over R.
  3. (0ii0) over C.
  4. (10000−1010) over R.
  5. (i10i) over C.

exr-normal-operators-b2.title: B2: The splitting of a singular normal operator
exr-normal-operators-b2.title_html: B2: The splitting of a singular normal operator
exr-normal-operators-b2.html:
Let C=(1−1001−1−101)∈M3(R), and let T=TC be the operator it defines on R3.

  1. Verify that T is normal.
  2. Compute kerT and kerT∗ and check that they agree.
  3. Compute imT, and verify directly that R3=kerT⊕imT with the two summands orthogonal, as @cor-normal-kernel (c) predicts.

exr-normal-operators-b3.title: B3: Triangular and normal, by hand
exr-normal-operators-b3.title_html: B3: Triangular and normal, by hand
exr-normal-operators-b3.html:
Let A=(ab0d)∈M2(C).

  1. Compute the (1,1) entries of A∗A and of AA∗.
  2. Hence prove that A is normal if and only if b=0, that is, if and only if A is diagonal.
  3. Which upper triangular matrices in M2(C) are unitary?

Hint: for (a), you only need one entry of each product.

exr-normal-operators-c1.title: C1: A normal operator with no proper invariant subspace
exr-normal-operators-c1.title_html: C1: A normal operator with no proper invariant subspace
exr-normal-operators-c1.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space with V≠{0}, and let T∈L(V) be normal. Suppose the only T-invariant subspaces of V are {0} and V.

  1. Show that dim⁡V=1.
  2. Show that the conclusion fails over R, by exhibiting a normal operator on R2 whose only invariant subspaces are {0} and R2.
  3. Where exactly does the argument of (a) use that the field is C?

Hint: an eigenvector spans an invariant subspace.

exr-normal-operators-c2.title: C2: Arithmetic of normal operators
exr-normal-operators-c2.html:
Let S,T∈L(V) be normal.

  1. Prove that T∗ is normal and that cT is normal for every c∈F.
  2. Prove that p(T) is normal for every polynomial p∈F[x].
  3. Give a concrete S and T, both normal, with ST not normal. (Part (b) shows that this cannot happen when S is a polynomial in T.)

exr-normal-operators-c3.title: C3: Normality depends on the inner product
exr-normal-operators-c3.title_html: C3: Normality depends on the inner product
exr-normal-operators-c3.html:
Normality is a property of T together with an inner product, not of T alone. Work on V=R2 with the operator T whose standard matrix is A=(0−110).

  1. Verify that T is normal for the standard inner product.
  2. Now use ⟨x,y⟩G=y⊤Gx with G=diag(1,2), which is an inner product on R2. Using the rule [T∗]EE=G−1A⊤G in the standard basis E (@exr-adjoints-c3), compute the matrix of the adjoint of T for this inner product.
  3. Show that T is not normal for ⟨⋅,⋅⟩G, and reconcile this with (a).

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-a1.title: A1
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-a1.html:
1. State the canonical form of an element of O(n), saying what the blocks are and which angles are allowed.
  2. Which hypothesis on Q turns the rotation-scaling blocks of the real normal form into rotation blocks, and why?
  3. Write down the cross-product matrix Kn and state the identity Kn3=? for a unit n.
  4. Given Q∈SO(3), how do you find its angle, and how do you find its axis? Name the two degenerate cases.
  5. True or false: if Q∈O(n) and detQ=1, then Q fixes a non-zero vector. Justify your answer.
  6. How many Householder reflections can be needed to write an element of O(n), and what does the parity of that number say?

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-b1.title: B1: Axis and angle
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-b1.html:
For each of the following, decide whether it lies in SO(3), O(3)∖SO(3), or neither. For those in SO(3), find the axis and the angle; for those in O(3) with determinant −1, give the canonical form [−1]⊕Rθ and say what the map is geometrically.

  1. 19(4−8141−8744).
  2. 19(−7444−1848−1).
  3. 19(7−4−4−41−8−4−81).
  4. 19(4−8141−8745).

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-b2.title: B2: Mirrors
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-b2.html:
1. Write the matrix M=(001010100) as a Householder reflection Hw, and say which plane is its mirror.
  2. Following the proof of @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small, write Q=(001100010) as a product of Householder reflections, and check the count against detQ.

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-b3.title: B3: Rodrigues in an example
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-b3.html:
1. Compute Re3,θ from Rodrigues’ formula and check that it is Rθ⊕[1].
  2. Compute Rn,2π/3 for n=13(1,1,1), and identify the resulting matrix.

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c1.title: C1: The plane, re-derived
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c1.html:
1. Use @thm-orthogonal-canonical-form to prove that every Q∈O(2) is either orthogonally similar to Rθ for a unique θ∈[0,π], or orthogonally similar to diag(1,−1).
  2. Chapter 10 proved more: Q equals Rθ or Mθ (@thm-orthogonal-2x2). Explain exactly what information (a) loses, and why the canonical form must lose it.
  3. Deduce that any two reflections of R2 are orthogonally similar, and that Rα and Rβ are orthogonally similar if and only if β=±α.

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c2.title: C2: Products of rotations
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c2.html:
1. Prove that the product of two rotations of R3 is a rotation of R3, and explain which theorem supplies the axis.
  2. Let A and B be the half-turns about two perpendicular axes span(a) and span(b), with a⊥b unit vectors. Prove that AB is the half-turn about the axis span(a×b).
  3. Deduce that every rotation of R3 is a product of two half-turns.

Hint for (c): use @thm-cartan-dieudonne-small, or the description of a half-turn in the Quick check after @thm-rodrigues.

exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c3.title: C3: Moving one point of the sphere to another
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c3.title_html: C3: Moving one point of the sphere to another
exr-orthogonal-matrices-and-rotations-c3.html:
Let S={x∈R3:‖x‖=1}.

  1. Prove that for all u,v∈S there is Q∈SO(3) with Qu=v. (One says that SO(3) acts transitively on S.)
  2. Prove that {Q∈SO(3):Qu=u}={Ru,θ:θ∈R}, and that this set is an abelian subgroup of SO(3).
  3. Is the analogue of (a) true for SO(2) acting on the unit circle of R2? And for SO(4) acting on the unit sphere of R4? Justify your answers.

exr-schur-triangularization-a1.title: A1
exr-schur-triangularization-a1.html:
1. State @thm-schur-triangularization, including the field and every hypothesis.
  2. In the proof, an eigenvector of T∗ is taken rather than one of T. Say why, in one sentence, and name the property of (span(v))⊥ that is wanted.
  3. True or false: if A∈Mn(C) is upper triangular in some orthonormal basis, then its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of that triangular matrix. Justify your answer.
  4. Which step of the proof of @thm-schur-triangularization fails over R?
  5. Give a matrix in M2(C) that is upper triangular in an orthonormal basis but is not diagonal in any.

exr-schur-triangularization-b1.title: B1: A Schur form with complex entries
exr-schur-triangularization-b1.title_html: B1: A Schur form with complex entries
exr-schur-triangularization-b1.html:
Let A=(12−13), regarded as a complex matrix.

  1. Find the eigenvalues of A.
  2. Find a unitary U∈M2(C) with U∗AU upper triangular, and compute that triangular matrix.
  3. Explain why no real orthogonal Q makes Q⊤AQ upper triangular.

exr-schur-triangularization-b2.title: B2: A three-by-three Schur form
exr-schur-triangularization-b2.html:
Let A=(211123004).

  1. Verify that (1,−1,0) is an eigenvector and find the corresponding eigenvalue.
  2. Extend it to an orthonormal basis of R3 and compute Q⊤AQ for the resulting Q.
  3. Hence write down the eigenvalues of A with their algebraic multiplicities.

exr-schur-triangularization-b3.title: B3: The field matters
exr-schur-triangularization-b3.html:
Let A=(a−bba)∈M2(R) with b≠0.

  1. Find the eigenvalues of A over C and show that A is unitarily similar to a diagonal matrix in M2(C).
  2. Prove that there is no invertible P∈M2(R) at all, orthogonal or otherwise, with P−1AP upper triangular.
  3. Say what @thm-real-schur produces for this A.

exr-schur-triangularization-c1.title: C1: Cayley–Hamilton from the triangular factors
exr-schur-triangularization-c1.title_html: C1: Cayley–Hamilton from the triangular factors
exr-schur-triangularization-c1.html:
Let T∈Mn(C) be upper triangular with diagonal entries λ1,…,λn, and set Nk=(T−λ1I)(T−λ2I)⋯(T−λkI) for 1≤k≤n.

  1. Prove by induction on k that the first k columns of Nk are zero.
  2. Deduce that pT(T)=0.
  3. Deduce the Cayley–Hamilton Theorem (@thm-cayley-hamilton) for every A∈Mn(C), using @cor-schur-matrix.

Hint for (a): the j-th column of T−λjI has its only possibly non-zero entries in rows 1,…,j−1.

exr-schur-triangularization-c2.title: C2: The Frobenius norm is unitarily invariant
exr-schur-triangularization-c2.title_html: C2: The Frobenius norm is unitarily invariant
exr-schur-triangularization-c2.html:
For A∈Mm×n(C) write ‖A‖F2:=∑i,j|aij|2; this is the norm induced by the Frobenius inner product ⟨A,B⟩=tr(B∗A) of Chapter 10, Section 1.

  1. Prove that ‖A‖F2=tr(A∗A).
  2. Prove that ‖UA‖F=‖A‖F=‖AV‖F whenever U∈Mm(C) and V∈Mn(C) are unitary.
  3. Deduce that if A=UTU∗ is a Schur factorization (@cor-schur-matrix), then ‖A‖F=‖T‖F.

exr-schur-triangularization-c3.title: C3: Distinct eigenvalues are dense, but not over the reals
exr-schur-triangularization-c3.title_html: C3: Distinct eigenvalues are dense, but not over the reals
exr-schur-triangularization-c3.html:
1. Sharpen @cor-schur-normal-matrix-nearby: prove that for every A∈Mn(C) and every ε>0 there is A′ with n distinct eigenvalues and |aij−aij′|<ε for all i,j.
  2. Show that the analogous statement fails over R: for R=(0−110) there is an ε>0 such that no real matrix within ε of R, entry by entry, has a real eigenvalue at all.

Hint for (b): a real 2×2 matrix with entries a,b,c,d has real eigenvalues exactly when (a−d)2+4bc≥0.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-a1.title: A1
exr-self-adjoint-operators-a1.html:
1. State what it means for T∈L(V) to be self-adjoint, in terms of T∗ and in terms of inner products, and say what the matrix condition is and in which bases it may be used.
  2. True or false: a symmetric matrix in M2(C) has real eigenvalues. Justify your answer.
  3. Which field does @thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue concern, and which earlier theorem supplies the eigenvalue it borrows?
  4. True or false: if T is self-adjoint and U is any subspace, then U⊥ is T-invariant. Justify your answer.
  5. State the difference between @thm-self-adjoint-zero-test and @thm-complex-zero-test, and give the standard example showing the second has no real analogue.
  6. Give a normal operator on R2 that is not self-adjoint.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-b1.title: B1: Determine which are self-adjoint
exr-self-adjoint-operators-b1.html:
Determine which of the following operators are self-adjoint. Justify your answer; for those that are not, exhibit a pair u,v with ⟨Tu,v⟩≠⟨u,Tv⟩, or compute T∗.

  1. TA on C2, A=(12+i2−i−5), standard inner product.
  2. TB on C2, B=(01−10), standard inner product.
  3. TC on R3, C=(120213031), standard inner product.
  4. S∗S, for an arbitrary S∈L(V,W) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces.
  5. PU−PU⊥, for a subspace U of a finite-dimensional V.
  6. T(x1,x2)=(x2,x1) on R2 with the standard inner product, whose matrix in the basis C=((1,0),(1,2)) is (−12321212), which is not symmetric.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-b2.title: B2: Eigenvalues and orthogonality
exr-self-adjoint-operators-b2.html:
1. For A=(0−ii0)∈M2(C), check that A is Hermitian, find its eigenvalues and an eigenvector for each, and verify that the eigenvectors are orthogonal.
  2. For S=(311131113)∈M3(R), find the eigenvalues with their multiplicities and bases of the eigenspaces, and verify that the two eigenspaces are orthogonal.
  3. Hence write down an orthonormal basis of R3 consisting of eigenvectors of S.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-b3.title: B3: A self-adjoint square root of zero
exr-self-adjoint-operators-b3.title_html: B3: A self-adjoint square root of zero
exr-self-adjoint-operators-b3.html: Let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint with T2=0. Prove that T=0. Deduce that a self-adjoint T with Tk=0 for some k≥1 is zero.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-c1.title: C1: The operator S^{*}S
exr-self-adjoint-operators-c1.title_html: C1: The operator S∗S
exr-self-adjoint-operators-c1.html:
Let S∈L(V,W) between finite-dimensional inner product spaces over F, and set T=S∗S∈L(V).

  1. Prove that T is self-adjoint and that ⟨Tv,v⟩≥0 for every v∈V, with equality if and only if Sv=0.
  2. Deduce that every eigenvalue of T is a non-negative real number.
  3. Prove that T is invertible if and only if S is injective.

Hint for (a): the quantity ⟨Tv,v⟩ is a norm squared in disguise.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-c2.title: C2: Sums and products
exr-self-adjoint-operators-c2.html:
Let S,T∈L(V) be self-adjoint.

  1. Prove that S+T and cT are self-adjoint for every real scalar c, and show by example that cT need not be self-adjoint for c∈C.
  2. Prove that ST is self-adjoint if and only if ST=TS.
  3. Give self-adjoint S,T∈L(C2) with ST not self-adjoint.

exr-self-adjoint-operators-c3.title: C3: What the real quadratic form does determine
exr-self-adjoint-operators-c3.title_html: C3: What the real quadratic form does determine
exr-self-adjoint-operators-c3.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over R and T∈L(V). Call T skew-adjoint if T∗=−T.

  1. Prove that ⟨Tv,v⟩=0 for every v∈V if and only if T is skew-adjoint.
  2. Deduce that every T∈L(V) can be written uniquely as T=A+B with A self-adjoint and B skew-adjoint, and that ⟨Tv,v⟩=⟨Av,v⟩ for every v.
  3. Conclude that over R the function v↦⟨Tv,v⟩ determines A and nothing about B. Contrast this with the complex case.

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: A1
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
1. Define the spectral resolution of T, and say which operators have one over C and which over R.
  2. List the properties of the family (P1,…,Pk) given by @thm-spectral-resolution, and say how many terms the resolution of a self-adjoint T∈L(R5) with eigenvalues 2,2,2,7,7 has.
  3. True or false: if T=μ1Q1+μ2Q2 with μ1≠μ2 and Q1,Q2 non-zero operators satisfying Qi2=Qi, Q1Q2=Q2Q1=0 and Q1+Q2=idV, then T is normal. Justify your answer.
  4. Define f(T) for a function f on spec(T), and say exactly how much information about f it uses.
  5. State @thm-functional-calculus-properties (a) and explain in one sentence why the rest of the section would be unusable without it.
  6. Give two different self-adjoint square roots of idV on R2, and say which one @thm-normal-square-root singles out and why.

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: B1: Write these as \sum\lambda_i\P_i
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title_html: B1: Write these as ∑λiPi
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
Find the spectral resolution of each of the following matrices, and check in each case that the projections are self-adjoint, idempotent, mutually annihilating and sum to I.

  1. A=(21−i1+i3)∈M2(C).
  2. S=(201030102)∈M3(R).
  3. U=12(1−111)∈M2(C).

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: B2: Computing through the resolution
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
Let C=(13121213)∈M2(R).

  1. Find the spectral resolution of C.
  2. Hence compute C, and verify by squaring.
  3. Hence give a closed formula for Cm and write down C100.
  4. Hence compute eC.

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: B3: Is it a spectral resolution?
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title_html: B3: Is it a spectral resolution?
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
Determine which of the following displays the spectral resolution of the operator TA on the stated space. Justify your answer; for those that do not, name the condition of @thm-spectral-resolution-unique that fails and say what the correct resolution is.

  1. On R2: A=(200−1), with μ1=2, Q1=(1000), μ2=−1, Q2=(0001).
  2. On R2: A=3I, with μ1=μ2=3, Q1=12(1111), Q2=12(1−1−11).
  3. On R2: A=(3101), with μ1=3, Q1=12(2100), μ2=1, Q2=12(0−102).

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: C1: The projections are polynomials in the operator
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title_html: C1: The projections are polynomials in the operator
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk∈F and resolution of the identity (P1,…,Pk).

  1. Prove that Pi=ℓi(T), where ℓi∈F[x] is the i-th Lagrange basis polynomial for the nodes λ1,…,λk.
  2. Deduce that for every f:spec(T)→F there is a polynomial p of degree less than k with f(T)=p(T).
  3. Deduce that every operator commuting with T commutes with each Pi, re-proving @thm-functional-calculus-properties (e) by a different route.

Hint for (a): @def-lagrange-basis produces a polynomial taking prescribed values at prescribed nodes.

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: C2: When the projections have rank one
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title_html: C2: When the projections have rank one
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), with dim⁡V=n and resolution of the identity (P1,…,Pk).

  1. Prove that rankPi=dim⁡Eλi(T) and that ∑irankPi=n.
  2. Deduce that every Pi has rank 1 if and only if T has n distinct eigenvalues.
  3. Suppose every Pi has rank 1. Prove that every S∈L(V) commuting with T is a polynomial in T.

exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title: C3: What the functional calculus forgets
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.title_html: C3: What the functional calculus forgets
exr-spectral-resolutions-and-functional-.html:
Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk, and let f,g:spec(T)→F.

  1. Prove that f(T)=0 if and only if f(λi)=0 for every i. Deduce that f(T)=g(T) if and only if f=g.
  2. Deduce that {p(T):p∈F[x]}=span(P1,…,Pk), a subspace of L(V) of dimension exactly k.
  3. Deduce that mT=(x−λ1)(x−λ2)⋯(x−λk), so that the minimal polynomial of an operator satisfying (∗) has no repeated root.

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-a1.title: A1
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-a1.html:
1. State the complex spectral theorem, including every hypothesis, and state its matrix form.
  2. What goes wrong with the proof if the field is R? Name the exact step.
  3. True or false: a matrix in Mn(C) with n distinct eigenvalues is unitarily diagonalizable. Justify your answer.
  4. Let A∈M3(C) be normal with spec(A)={2,2,−1} as a list with multiplicity. Is the unitary U in A=UDU∗ determined by A and the order of D? What is determined?
  5. A normal operator T satisfies T∗=T3. What can you say about its eigenvalues?
  6. Explain why @lem-triangular-normal-diagonal cannot be weakened to “a normal matrix with some of its below-diagonal entries zero is diagonal”.

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-b1.title: B1: Unitarily diagonalize
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-b1.html:
For each matrix, find a unitary U and a diagonal D with U∗AU=D.

  1. A=(3−ii3).
  2. A=12(1ii1).

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-b2.title: B2: A circulant, diagonalized
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-b2.html:
Let ω=e2πi/3, so ω3=1 and 1+ω+ω2=0, and let C=(110011101)∈M3(C).

  1. Verify that C is normal.
  2. Show that fj=13(1,ωj,ω2j) is an eigenvector of C for j=0,1,2, and find the eigenvalue.
  3. Deduce a unitary F with F∗CF diagonal, and write down the diagonal explicitly.

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-b3.title: B3: Decide unitary diagonalizability
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-b3.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are unitarily diagonalizable over C, and which are merely diagonalizable. Justify your answer.

  1. (01−10).
  2. (2302).
  3. (1203).
  4. (010001100).

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-c1.title: C1: Operators of finite order
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-c1.html:
Let T∈L(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, and suppose Tk=idV for some integer k≥1.

  1. Prove that every eigenvalue of T is a k-th root of unity.
  2. Deduce that T is unitary and unitarily diagonalizable.
  3. Show that the hypothesis “normal” cannot be dropped from (b) by exhibiting a T with T2=idV that is not unitary.

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-c2.title: C2: Same spectrum, same multiplicities
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(C) be normal, and suppose they have the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, that is, the same characteristic polynomial.

  1. Prove that there is a unitary W with B=WAW∗ (one says A and B are unitarily similar).
  2. Give two matrices in M2(C) with the same characteristic polynomial that are not unitarily similar, and say which hypothesis of (a) they violate.
  3. Deduce that two normal matrices are unitarily similar if and only if they are similar.

exr-spectral-theorem-complex-c3.title: C3: Normality cannot be dropped
exr-spectral-theorem-complex-c3.html:
@cor-normal-spectral-corollaries reads the class of a normal operator off its spectrum. This exercise shows that each part fails without that hypothesis.

  1. Give A∈M2(C) with both eigenvalues real that is not Hermitian.
  2. Give A∈M2(C) with both eigenvalues of modulus 1 that is not unitary.
  3. Over R, give A∈M2(R) with ⟨Ax,x⟩≥0 for every x∈R2 whose eigenvalues are not non-negative reals. Why does no such example exist over C?

exr-spectral-theorem-real-a1.title: A1
exr-spectral-theorem-real-a1.html:
1. State the real spectral theorem and its matrix form, with every hypothesis.
  2. Which two results from Section 2 does the induction use, and what does each one supply?
  3. True or false: a normal operator on a real inner product space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Justify your answer.
  4. What are the possible diagonal blocks in the real normal form of a normal operator, and what does the condition b>0 rule out?
  5. Given a symmetric A with orthonormal eigenvectors q1,q2 and eigenvalues 9 and 1, describe the curve x⊤Ax=1.
  6. True or false: a real matrix with real eigenvalues is symmetric. Justify your answer.

exr-spectral-theorem-real-b1.title: B1: Orthogonally diagonalize
exr-spectral-theorem-real-b1.html:
For each symmetric matrix, find an orthogonal Q and a diagonal D with Q⊤AQ=D.

  1. A=(1221).
  2. A=(401020104).

exr-spectral-theorem-real-b2.title: B2: Identify the conic
exr-spectral-theorem-real-b2.html: Identify the curve 5x2+4xy+5y2=1: say what kind of conic it is, find its axes, and find their half-lengths.

exr-spectral-theorem-real-b3.title: B3: A sum of rank-one projections
exr-spectral-theorem-real-b3.title_html: B3: A sum of rank-one projections
exr-spectral-theorem-real-b3.html: Using your answer to @exr-spectral-theorem-real-b1 (b), write A=(401020104) as ∑iλiqiqi⊤, with the three matrices qiqi⊤ written out, and verify the identity by adding them.

exr-spectral-theorem-real-c1.title: C1: One eigenvalue only
exr-spectral-theorem-real-c1.html:
1. Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric with every eigenvalue equal to λ. Prove that A=λI.
  2. Show that (a) fails without symmetry, by exhibiting a matrix in M2(R) whose only eigenvalue is 0 and which is not 0.
  3. Deduce that a symmetric A with A2=A is the matrix of an orthogonal projection.

exr-spectral-theorem-real-c2.title: C2: Diagonalizing two matrices at once
exr-spectral-theorem-real-c2.title_html: C2: Diagonalizing two matrices at once
exr-spectral-theorem-real-c2.html:
Let A,B∈Mn(R) be symmetric with AB=BA.

  1. Prove that each eigenspace Eλ(A) is B-invariant, and that the restriction of TB to it is self-adjoint.
  2. Prove that there is a single Q∈O(n) with Q⊤AQ and Q⊤BQ both diagonal.
  3. Show that the conclusion fails without commutativity, using (1000) and (0110).

Hint for (b): apply @thm-spectral-real inside each eigenspace of A.

exr-spectral-theorem-real-c3.title: C3: A rotation-scaling in normal form
exr-spectral-theorem-real-c3.title_html: C3: A rotation-scaling in normal form
exr-spectral-theorem-real-c3.html:
Let A=(34−43)∈M2(R).

  1. Verify that A is normal and not symmetric, and find its complex eigenvalues.
  2. Find an orthogonal Q with Q⊤AQ=Λ(λ) for the eigenvalue λ with positive imaginary part.
  3. Explain why no orthogonal Q makes Q⊤AQ diagonal, and why this does not contradict @thm-spectral-complex.

exr-sylvester-equation-a1.title: A1
exr-sylvester-equation-a1.html:
1. Define the Sylvester operator of a pair (A,B) with A∈Mm(F), B∈Mn(F), and state the dimension of the space it acts on.
  2. Write down the matrix of the Sylvester operator with respect to the vectorization vec, and say which Chapter 7 result produces it.
  3. State the criterion for AX−XB=C to have exactly one solution for every C, over C.
  4. True or false: if AX−XB=C has at least one solution for every C, then that solution is unique. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if spec(A)∩spec(B)=∅, then AX+XB=C has exactly one solution for every C. Justify your answer.

exr-sylvester-equation-b1.title: B1: A Sylvester equation by vectorization
exr-sylvester-equation-b1.title_html: B1: A Sylvester equation by vectorization
exr-sylvester-equation-b1.html:
Over Q, let A=(3101),B=(−1010),C=(210−2).

  1. Compute spec(A) and spec(B), and decide whether AX−XB=C has exactly one solution.
  2. Write down K=I2⊗A−B⊤⊗I2, and check that its diagonal entries are the four differences λi−μj.
  3. Solve the equation.

exr-sylvester-equation-b2.title: B2: Block-diagonalizing a 3 × 3 matrix
exr-sylvester-equation-b2.html:
Let M=(212023005)∈M3(Q).

  1. Partition M as 3=2+1, name the blocks A, B, C, and explain why @cor-block-diagonalization applies.
  2. Solve the corresponding Sylvester equation.
  3. Write down P and verify that P−1MP=A⊕B.

exr-sylvester-equation-b3.title: B3: Which equations are uniquely solvable?
exr-sylvester-equation-b3.title_html: B3: Which equations are uniquely solvable?
exr-sylvester-equation-b3.html:
Determine, for each of the following, whether the stated equation has exactly one solution X∈M2(C) for every right-hand side C∈M2(C). Justify your answer.

  1. AX−XB=C with A=(1101), B=(2003).
  2. AX−XB=C with A=(01−10), B=(0−110).
  3. AX+XB=C with A=(1002), B=(−1503).
  4. AX−XB=C with A=(1101), B=(1021).
  5. AX−XB=C with A∈M2(C) nilpotent and B∈M2(C) invertible.

exr-sylvester-equation-c1.title: C1: Eigenvectors of the Sylvester operator
exr-sylvester-equation-c1.title_html: C1: Eigenvectors of the Sylvester operator
exr-sylvester-equation-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C), and let S=SA,B.

  1. Suppose Ax=λx with x∈Cm non-zero, and suppose y∈Cn is a left eigenvector of B for μ, so that y⊤B=μy⊤ (@def-left-eigenvector). Prove that xy⊤≠0 and that S(xy⊤)=(λ−μ)xy⊤.
  2. Deduce that every difference λ−μ with λ∈spec(A) and μ∈spec(B) is an eigenvalue of S.
  3. Hence give a second proof that S is not invertible when A and B have a common eigenvalue, one that uses no Kronecker products.

exr-sylvester-equation-c2.title: C2: The kernel when the spectra meet
exr-sylvester-equation-c2.title_html: C2: The kernel when the spectra meet
exr-sylvester-equation-c2.html:
Let A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C) have eigenvalue lists λ1,…,λm and μ1,…,μn with algebraic multiplicity, and let d=#{(i,j):λi=μj}.

  1. Prove that dim⁡kerSA,B≥1 if and only if d≥1.
  2. Prove that dim⁡kerSA,B≤d.
  3. Show that the inequality in (b) can be strict, by computing kerSA,B for A=B=J2(0).

exr-sylvester-equation-c3.title: C3: Only the scalars commute with everything
exr-sylvester-equation-c3.title_html: C3: Only the scalars commute with everything
exr-sylvester-equation-c3.html:
Let F be a field, n≥2, and let Eij∈Mn(F) be the matrix unit with 1 in position (i,j) and 0 elsewhere.

  1. Suppose A∈Mn(F) satisfies AEij=EijA for all i≠j. Prove that A=cIn for some c∈F.
  2. Deduce that the only matrices commuting with every X∈Mn(F) are the scalar matrices, that is, kerSA,A=Mn(F) forces A scalar.
  3. Deduce that the only matrices commuting with every invertible matrix are again the scalar matrices.

Hint for (c): In+Eij is invertible when i≠j.

lem-adjoint-eigenline-complement.title: Eigenvectors of the Adjoint Cut Out Invariant Subspaces
lem-adjoint-eigenline-complement.title_html: Eigenvectors of the Adjoint Cut Out Invariant Subspaces
lem-adjoint-eigenline-complement.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F, let T∈L(V), and let W⊆V be a T∗-invariant subspace. Then W⊥ is T-invariant.

lem-cross-matrix-properties.title: Properties of the Cross-product Matrix
lem-cross-matrix-properties.html:
Let n∈R3 with ‖n‖=1, and write K=Kn. Then

  1. K⊤=−K and Kn=0;
  2. K2=nn⊤−I3, so K2 is symmetric and K2v=−v for every v⊥n;
  3. K3=−K;
  4. for every v⊥n: ‖Kv‖=‖v‖, Kv⊥v and Kv⊥n.

lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant.title: Unitary Invariance of the Frobenius Norm
lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant.title_html: Unitary Invariance of the Frobenius Norm
lem-frobenius-unitarily-invariant.html: Let A∈Mm×n(C), let U∈U(m) and let V∈U(n). Then ‖UA‖F=‖A‖F=‖AV‖F. In particular, if A is square and U is unitary then ‖U∗AU‖F=‖A‖F.

lem-kronecker-sum-spectrum.title: The Eigenvalues of a Kronecker Sum
lem-kronecker-sum-spectrum.title_html: The Eigenvalues of a Kronecker Sum
lem-kronecker-sum-spectrum.html: Let A∈Mm(C) with eigenvalues λ1,…,λm and let B∈Mn(C) with eigenvalues μ1,…,μn, each list repeated according to algebraic multiplicity. Then the mn eigenvalues of K=In⊗A−B⊤⊗Im∈Mmn(C), listed with algebraic multiplicity, are the mn differences λi−μj (1≤i≤m, 1≤j≤n).

lem-reflection-swaps-vectors.title: A Mirror Between Two Vectors of Equal Length
lem-reflection-swaps-vectors.title_html: A Mirror Between Two Vectors of Equal Length
lem-reflection-swaps-vectors.html: Let x,y∈Rn with ‖x‖=‖y‖ and x≠y. Then w:=x−y is non-zero and Hwx=y.

lem-triangular-normal-diagonal.title: A Normal Triangular Matrix Is Diagonal
lem-triangular-normal-diagonal.title_html: A Normal Triangular Matrix Is Diagonal
lem-triangular-normal-diagonal.html: Let T=(tij)∈Mn(C) be upper triangular and normal. Then T is diagonal.

prp-normal-invariant-reducing.title: An Invariant Subspace of a Normal Operator Is Reducing
prp-normal-invariant-reducing.title_html: An Invariant Subspace of a Normal Operator Is Reducing
prp-normal-invariant-reducing.html: Let T∈L(V) be normal on a finite-dimensional inner product space, and let U⊆V be T-invariant. Then U is T∗-invariant, U⊥ is T-invariant, and T|U is a normal operator on U.

thm-cartan-dieudonne-small.title: Reflections Generate the Orthogonal Group
thm-cartan-dieudonne-small.html: Let n≥1 and Q∈O(n). Then Q is a product of at most n Householder reflections. (The identity is the empty product, of zero reflections.)

thm-circulant-diagonalization.title: Circulant Diagonalization
thm-circulant-diagonalization.html: Let C∈Mn(C) be the circulant with first row c and symbol pc. Then every Fourier vector is an eigenvector of C, Cfj=pc(ωj)fj(j=0,1,…,n−1), and consequently F∗CF=diag(pc(1), pc(ω), …, pc(ωn−1)). The same unitary F works for every circulant of size n, and detC=∏j=0n−1pc(ωj).

thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift.title: Circulants Are Exactly the Polynomials in the Shift
thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift.title_html: Circulants Are Exactly the Polynomials in the Shift
thm-circulant-is-polynomial-in-shift.html:
Let c∈Cn and let C be the circulant with first row c, with symbol pc. Then:

  1. C=pc(S); conversely, q(S) is a circulant for every q∈C[x].
  2. C∗ is the circulant with first row (c0―,cn−1―,cn−2―,…,c1―).
  3. C is normal, and any two circulants of the same size commute.

thm-commuting-normal-sum-normal.title: Sums and Products of Commuting Normal Operators
thm-commuting-normal-sum-normal.title_html: Sums and Products of Commuting Normal Operators
thm-commuting-normal-sum-normal.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let S,T∈L(V) be normal with ST=TS. Then S+T and ST are normal.

thm-complex-zero-test.title: The Zero Test over the Complex Numbers
thm-complex-zero-test.title_html: The Zero Test over the Complex Numbers
thm-complex-zero-test.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let T∈L(V) be any operator. If ⟨Tv,v⟩=0 for every v∈V, then T=0.

thm-convolution-theorem.title: Convolution Theorem
thm-convolution-theorem.html:
Let c,d∈Cn with circulants C,C′ and symbols pc,pd. Then:

  1. CC′ is the circulant with first row c∗d;
  2. for every j, pc∗d(ωj)=pc(ωj)pd(ωj).

In words: convolving the first rows corresponds to multiplying the eigenvalue lists entry by entry.

thm-fourier-matrix-unitary.title: The Fourier Matrix Is Unitary
thm-fourier-matrix-unitary.html: The list (f0,f1,…,fn−1) is an orthonormal basis of Cn. Equivalently, the Fourier matrix F:=1n(11⋯11ω⋯ωn−1⋮⋮⋮1ωn−1⋯ω(n−1)2),(F)mj=ωmjn, whose j-th column is fj, is unitary: F∗F=FF∗=I.

thm-functional-calculus-properties.title: Properties of the Functional Calculus
thm-functional-calculus-properties.html:
Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk and resolution of the identity (P1,…,Pk). Let f,g:spec(T)→F and c∈F, with f+g, cf and fg taken pointwise.

  1. (Compatibility) For every p∈F[x], the operator p(T) of @def-polynomial-of-operator equals ∑ip(λi)Pi; that is, it agrees with @def-function-of-normal-operator applied to the restriction of p to spec(T).
  2. (Algebra homomorphism) (f+g)(T)=f(T)+g(T), (cf)(T)=cf(T), (fg)(T)=f(T)g(T)=g(T)f(T), and 1(T)=idV.
  3. (Adjoints) f(T)∗=f―(T), where f―(λ)=f(λ)―. In particular f(T) is self-adjoint when f is real-valued, and unitary when |f(λi)|=1 for every i.
  4. (Spectral mapping) f(T) satisfies (∗), with the same orthonormal eigenbasis as T, and spec(f(T))=f(spec(T)).
  5. (Commutation) If S∈L(V) commutes with T, then S commutes with every Pi and hence with f(T). In particular T and f(T) commute.

thm-normal-characterizations.title: Characterizations of Normality
thm-normal-characterizations.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent.

  1. T is normal.
  2. ‖Tv‖=‖T∗v‖ for every v∈V.
  3. ⟨Tu,Tv⟩=⟨T∗u,T∗v⟩ for all u,v∈V.

Suppose in addition that F=C, and set A=12(T+T∗),B=12i(T−T∗), so that A and B are self-adjoint and T=A+iB. Then (a)–(c) are further equivalent to

  1. AB=BA.

thm-normal-eigenvector-shared.title: An Eigenvector of a Normal Operator Is an Eigenvector of Its Adjoint
thm-normal-eigenvector-shared.title_html: An Eigenvector of a Normal Operator Is an Eigenvector of Its Adjoint
thm-normal-eigenvector-shared.html: Let T∈L(V) be normal, let λ∈F and let v∈V. Then Tv=λvif and only ifT∗v=λ―v. In particular Eλ(T)=Eλ―(T∗), and λ∈spec(T) if and only if λ―∈spec(T∗).

thm-normal-powers.title: A Normal Operator Has No Hidden Kernel
thm-normal-powers.title_html: A Normal Operator Has No Hidden Kernel
thm-normal-powers.html: Let T∈L(V) be normal. Then kerTk=kerT for every integer k≥1. In particular, a normal nilpotent operator is the zero operator.

thm-normal-square-root.title: The Square Root of a Non-negative Normal Operator
thm-normal-square-root.title_html: The Square Root of a Non-negative Normal Operator
thm-normal-square-root.html:
Let V be a non-zero finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗) with spec(T)⊆[0,∞). Then there is exactly one operator S∈L(V) such that

  1. S satisfies (∗);
  2. spec(S)⊆[0,∞);
  3. S2=T.

It is S=∑iλiPi, where T=∑iλiPi is the spectral resolution of T. This S is self-adjoint, and it commutes with every operator that commutes with T.

thm-normal-tfae.title: Normality: The Complete List
thm-normal-tfae.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with algebraic multiplicity, and put H=12(A+A∗),K=12i(A−A∗), both of which are Hermitian, with A=H+iK. The following are equivalent.

  1. A∗A=AA∗, that is, A is normal.
  2. ‖Ax‖=‖A∗x‖ for every x∈Cn.
  3. ⟨Ax,Ay⟩=⟨A∗x,A∗y⟩ for all x,y∈Cn.
  4. HK=KH.
  5. Cn has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of A.
  6. A=UDU∗ for some unitary U and some diagonal D.
  7. A∗=p(A) for some polynomial p∈C[x].
  8. ∑i=1n|λi|2=‖A‖F2.

thm-normal-trace-criterion.title: Normality as a Trace Identity
thm-normal-trace-criterion.html: Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then A is normal if and only if tr(A∗A)=∑i=1n|λi|2.

thm-orthogonal-canonical-form.title: Canonical Form of an Orthogonal Matrix
thm-orthogonal-canonical-form.title_html: Canonical Form of an Orthogonal Matrix
thm-orthogonal-canonical-form.html: Let Q∈O(n). Then there are integers p,q,m≥0 with p+q+2m=n, and angles θ1,…,θm with 0<θj<π, and a matrix P∈O(n), such that P⊤QP=Ip⊕(−Iq)⊕Rθ1⊕⋯⊕Rθm. Moreover detQ=(−1)q, and p, q and the multiset {θ1,…,θm} are determined by Q.

thm-principal-axes.title: Principal Axis Theorem
thm-principal-axes.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric, let q(x)=x⊤Ax, and let Q∈O(n) with Q⊤AQ=D=diag(λ1,…,λn), the columns q1,…,qn of Q being an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Substituting x=Qy, that is, taking yi=⟨x,qi⟩ to be the coordinates of x in that basis, q(x)=∑i=1nλiyi2. In particular, for n=2 with λ1,λ2>0, the level set {q=1} is an ellipse whose axes lie along q1 and q2, with half-lengths 1/λ1 and 1/λ2.

thm-real-normal-form.title: Real Normal Form of a Normal Operator
thm-real-normal-form.title_html: Real Normal Form of a Normal Operator
thm-real-normal-form.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over R and let T∈L(V) be normal. Then V has an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of T is block diagonal, (c1)⊕⋯⊕(cp)⊕Λ(λ1)⊕⋯⊕Λ(λq), with c1,…,cp∈R and, for each j, λj=aj+bji with bj>0 and Λ(λj)=(aj−bjbjaj) the rotation-scaling block of @def-real-jordan-block. In matrix form: A∈Mn(R) is normal if and only if A=QBQ⊤ with Q∈O(n) and B of the displayed shape.

thm-real-schur.title: Real Schur Form
thm-real-schur.html: Let A∈Mn(R) with n≥1. Then there are an orthogonal Q∈O(n) and a matrix T∈Mn(R) with A=QTQ⊤, where T is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks of size 1×1 and 2×2, and every 2×2 diagonal block has a conjugate pair of non-real eigenvalues.

thm-rodrigues.title: Rodrigues’ Rotation Formula
thm-rodrigues.html:
Let n∈R3 be a unit vector, let θ∈R, and write K=Kn. Define Rn,θ:=I3+sin⁡θK+(1−cos⁡θ)K2.

  1. For every v∈R3, Rn,θv=⟨v,n⟩n+cos⁡θ(v−⟨v,n⟩n)+sin⁡θ(n×v).
  2. Rn,θn=n, and for every unit w⊥n the list B=(n,w,n×w) is an orthonormal basis of R3 with [TRn,θ]B=[1]⊕Rθ. In particular Rn,θ∈SO(3).
  3. Conversely, every Q∈SO(3) equals Rn,θ for some unit vector n and some θ∈[0,π].

thm-rotation-angle-trace.title: Axis and Angle from the Matrix
thm-rotation-angle-trace.title_html: Axis and Angle from the Matrix
thm-rotation-angle-trace.html:
Let Q=Rn,θ∈SO(3) with n a unit vector and θ∈[0,π]. Then

  1. trQ=1+2cos⁡θ, so cos⁡θ=12(trQ−1) and θ is determined by Q;
  2. Q−Q⊤=2sin⁡θKn;
  3. if 0<θ<π, then sin⁡θ>0 and n=12sin⁡θ(q32−q23, q13−q31, q21−q12); if θ=0 then Q=I3 and the axis is arbitrary; and if θ=π then Q+I3=2nn⊤, whose non-zero columns are the multiples 2nin of n.

thm-schur-inequality.title: Schur’s Inequality
thm-schur-inequality.html: Let A∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with algebraic multiplicity. Then ∑i=1n|λi|2≤‖A‖F2, with equality if and only if A is normal.

thm-schur-triangularization.title: Schur’s Unitary Triangularization
thm-schur-triangularization.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over C with dim⁡V=n≥1, and let T∈L(V).

  1. There is an orthonormal basis B of V such that [T]BB is upper triangular.
  2. More precisely, let λ1,…,λn be the eigenvalues of T, each listed as often as its algebraic multiplicity, in any order we please. Then B can be chosen so that the i-th diagonal entry of [T]BB is λi.

thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue.title: Real Self-adjoint Operators Have an Eigenvalue
thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue.title_html: Real Self-adjoint Operators Have an Eigenvalue
thm-self-adjoint-has-eigenvalue.html:
Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional inner product space over R and let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint. Then:

  1. every root of pT in C is real, so pT splits over R;
  2. T has an eigenvalue.

thm-self-adjoint-invariant-complement.title: Self-adjointness Passes to Orthogonal Complements
thm-self-adjoint-invariant-complement.html:
Let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint and let U⊆V be a T-invariant subspace. Then:

  1. U⊥ is T-invariant;
  2. T|U∈L(U) and T|U⊥∈L(U⊥) are self-adjoint, for the inner products inherited from V.

thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces.title: Distinct Eigenvalues Give Orthogonal Eigenvectors
thm-self-adjoint-orthogonal-eigenspaces.html: Let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint, and let u,v∈V satisfy Tu=λu and Tv=μv with λ≠μ. Then ⟨u,v⟩=0. Consequently Eλ(T)⊥Eμ(T) for distinct eigenvalues λ,μ.

thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues.title: Self-adjoint Operators Have Real Eigenvalues
thm-self-adjoint-real-eigenvalues.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F=R or F=C and let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint. Then every eigenvalue of T is real.

thm-self-adjoint-zero-test.title: The Zero Test for Self-adjoint Operators
thm-self-adjoint-zero-test.title_html: The Zero Test for Self-adjoint Operators
thm-self-adjoint-zero-test.html: Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F=R or F=C and let T∈L(V) be self-adjoint. If ⟨Tv,v⟩=0 for every v∈V, then T=0.

thm-shift-eigenvectors.title: Eigenvectors of the Cyclic Shift
thm-shift-eigenvectors.html: For j=0,1,…,n−1 let fj:=1n(1, ωj, ω2j, …, ω(n−1)j)∈Cn, that is, (fj)m=ωjm/n. Then Sfj=ωjfj. Consequently S is a unitary matrix with the n distinct eigenvalues 1,ω,…,ωn−1, and each eigenspace Eωj(S) is the line span(fj).

thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization.title: One Orthonormal Eigenbasis for a Commuting Family
thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization.title_html: One Orthonormal Eigenbasis for a Commuting Family
thm-simultaneous-unitary-diagonalization.html:
Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let F⊆L(V) be a non-empty commuting family of normal operators. Then V has an orthonormal basis B each of whose vectors is an eigenvector of every T∈F; equivalently, [T]B is diagonal for every T∈F.

Conversely, if some orthonormal basis B makes every [T]B diagonal, then F is commuting and every member of F is normal.

thm-simultaneous-unitary-triangularizati.title: Simultaneous Unitary Triangularization
thm-simultaneous-unitary-triangularizati.html: Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let F⊆L(V) be a non-empty commuting family. Then there is an orthonormal basis B of V such that [T]B is upper triangular for every T∈F. In particular, if A1,…,Ar∈Mn(C) commute pairwise, there is U∈U(n) with every U∗AiU upper triangular.

thm-spectral-complex.title: Complex Spectral Theorem
thm-spectral-complex.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over C and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent.

  1. T is normal.
  2. V has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of T.

thm-spectral-real.title: Real Spectral Theorem
thm-spectral-real.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over R and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent.

  1. T is self-adjoint.
  2. V has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of T.

thm-spectral-resolution.title: The Spectral Resolution and Its Projections
thm-spectral-resolution.title_html: The Spectral Resolution and Its Projections
thm-spectral-resolution.html:
Let T∈L(V) satisfy (∗), with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk, eigenspaces Ei=Eλi(T) and Pi=PEi. Then:

  1. V=E1⊕⋯⊕Ek, and Ei⊥Ej whenever i≠j;
  2. Pi∗=Pi and Pi2=Pi for every i, and PiPj=0 whenever i≠j;
  3. P1+⋯+Pk=idV;
  4. T=λ1P1+⋯+λkPk;
  5. TPi=PiT=λiPi for every i.

thm-spectral-resolution-unique.title: Uniqueness of the Spectral Resolution
thm-spectral-resolution-unique.html:
Let V be a non-zero finite-dimensional inner product space over F and let T∈L(V). Suppose T=μ1Q1+μ2Q2+⋯+μmQm, where μ1,…,μm∈F are distinct and Q1,…,Qm∈L(V) are non-zero operators satisfying

  1. Qi∗=Qi and Qi2=Qi for every i;
  2. QiQj=0 whenever i≠j;
  3. Q1+⋯+Qm=idV.

Then T satisfies (∗), spec(T)={μ1,…,μm}, and Qi is the orthogonal projection onto Eμi(T) for every i. In particular m is the number of distinct eigenvalues of T, and the given decomposition is the spectral resolution of T.

thm-sylvester-equation.title: Sylvester’s Theorem
thm-sylvester-equation.html:
Let A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C). The following are equivalent.

  1. spec(A)∩spec(B)=∅: the two matrices have no common eigenvalue.
  2. The Sylvester operator SA,B:X↦AX−XB is invertible on Mm×n(C).
  3. For every C∈Mm×n(C), the equation AX−XB=C has exactly one solution X.
  4. The only X∈Mm×n(C) with AX=XB is X=0.

thm-unitary-exponential.title: Unitary Matrices Are Exponentials of Hermitian Matrices
thm-unitary-exponential.title_html: Unitary Matrices Are Exponentials of Hermitian Matrices
thm-unitary-exponential.html:
Let n≥1.

  1. If A∈Mn(C) is normal with spectral resolution A=∑iλiPi, then eA=∑ieλiPi.
  2. If H∈Mn(C) is Hermitian, then eiH∈U(n), and deteiH=eitrH.
  3. Conversely, every U∈U(n) equals eiH for some Hermitian H, which may be chosen with spec(H)⊆[0,2π).
